note.explanation: For free fall, use the equations of motion with acceleration replaced by g. Take g = 10 m s⁻² downward as positive. If an object is thrown upward, take g = −10 m s⁻².
examples: A body dropped from rest for 3 s falls 45 m: S = 0 × 3 + ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m.
An arrow thrown upward at 30 m s⁻¹ takes 3 s to reach its highest point: 0 = 30 − 10t, so t = 3 s.
note.checkAnswer: For a body dropped from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = 10 m s⁻² downward.
note.simple: A freely falling object speeds up because Earth’s gravity pulls it downward. Use g = 10 m s⁻², and choose signs to match the direction of motion.
note.checkQuestion: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its initial velocity, and which way is g positive?
note.title: Using equations for free fall
steps: Write down the known values, including the direction of motion.
Use vᵢ = 0 if the object is released from rest.
Take g as positive downward; for an object thrown upward, take g as negative.
Choose the equation of motion that contains the unknown you need.
Substitute the values and give the answer with its unit.
note.answer: For a freely falling object released from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = +10 m s⁻² when downward is positive.

rationales: This is not correct; substituting t = 1 s into S = ½gt² does not give 10 m.
Correct: S = ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 m.
This is not correct; it is twice the distance found using S = ½gt².
This is not correct; it is eight times the distance found using S = ½gt².

mcqs.stem: A body is dropped from rest. What is its velocity after 1 s? Take downward as positive and g = 10 m s⁻².
rationales: This is not correct; gravity changes the body's velocity during the second.
Correct: v_f = v_i + gt = 0 + 10 × 1 = 10 m s⁻¹ downward.
This is not correct; 5 m is the distance fallen in 1 s, not the velocity.

mcqs.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 30 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to reach its highest point? Take g = −10 m s⁻².
rationales: Correct: at the highest point v_f = 0, so 0 = 30 − 10t and t = 3 s.
This is not correct; substituting t = 2 s gives a velocity that is still upward.
This is not correct; the ball would already have reached its highest point after 3 s.
This is not correct; it does not follow from v_f = v_i + gt with v_f = 0.

mcqs.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 30 m s⁻¹. What maximum height does it rise above its starting point? Take g = −10 m s⁻².
rationales: Correct: 2gS = v_f² − v_i² gives S = (0 − 30²) ÷ (2 × −10) = 45 m.
This is not correct; 30 is the initial velocity, not the maximum height.
This is not correct; it is twice the height obtained from the third equation of motion.
This is not correct; it is half the height obtained from the third equation of motion.

rationales: This is not correct; the object is thrown upward with an initial velocity.
Correct: the object's velocity is momentarily zero at the highest point.

written.text: An iron bob is dropped from the top of a tower. It reaches the ground in 4 seconds. Find: (a) the height of the tower (b) the velocity of the ball as it strikes the ground.

rubric.why: Correctly identifying the initial conditions and acceleration sets the sign convention and values.
rubric.description: State the known values for the falling body.
rubric.how: Write vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻² and t = 4 s.

rubric.why: The height is found using the second equation of motion.
rubric.description: Find the height of the tower.
rubric.how: Substitute in S = vᵢt + ½gt² and obtain 80 m.

rubric.why: The impact velocity is found using the first equation of motion.
rubric.description: Find the velocity as the ball strikes the ground.
rubric.how: Use v_f = vᵢ + gt and obtain 40 m s⁻¹ downward.

modelAnswer: For freely falling body: vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻², t = 4 s, S = h = ?, v_f = ?
(a) According to second equation of motion, S = vᵢt + ½gt²
Putting the values, h = 0 × 4 + ½ × 10 × (4)² = 80 m
(b) From the first equation of motion, v_f = vᵢ + gt
Putting the values, v_f = 0 + 10 × 4 = 40 m s⁻¹ downward
Answer: (a) 80 m (b) 40 m s⁻¹ downward

written.text: An arrow is thrown vertically upward with the help of a bow. The velocity of the arrow when it leaves the bow is 30 m s⁻¹. Determine time to reach the highest point? Also, find the maximum height attained by the arrow.

rubric.why: The upward direction requires gravitational acceleration to be negative, and velocity is zero at the highest point.
rubric.description: Identify the velocities and acceleration with the correct signs.
rubric.how: State vᵢ = 30 m s⁻¹, v_f = 0 and g = −10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: The first equation gives the time to the highest point.
rubric.description: Calculate the time using the first equation of motion.
rubric.how: Use v_f = vᵢ + gt to obtain t = 3 s.

rubric.why: The third equation of motion gives the maximum upward displacement.
rubric.description: Calculate the maximum height.
rubric.how: Use 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ² to obtain 45 m.

modelAnswer: Here, acceleration will be taken as negative, for the arrow is thrown vertically upward.
Initial velocity = vᵢ = 30 m s⁻¹; final velocity = v_f = 0; acceleration = g = −10 m s⁻²
From first equation of motion: v_f = vᵢ + gt
t = (v_f − vᵢ)/(−g)
Putting the values, t = (0 − 30)/−10 = 3 s
Now from the third equation of motion: 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ²
S = (v_f² − vᵢ²)/2(−g)
Putting the values, h = (0 − 30²)/(2 × 10) = 45 m
Answer: time = 3 s; maximum height = 45 m

written.text: Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?
written.finalAnswer: No. A heavier object will not fall faster; freely falling objects have the same acceleration due to gravity.

rubric.why: The answer must correctly state whether the heavier object falls faster.
rubric.description: Give a clear yes or no.
rubric.how: State that it does not imply the heavier object falls faster.

rubric.why: The explanation must connect the conclusion to the shared gravitational acceleration.
rubric.description: Explain using free-fall acceleration.
rubric.how: State that freely falling objects have the same acceleration due to gravity.

modelAnswer: No. Freely falling objects near Earth have the same constant acceleration due to gravity, so a heavier object does not fall faster than a lighter object.

written.text: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
written.finalAnswer: Replace a with g in the equations of motion; take g positive downward and take quantities in the opposite direction as negative. For a body released from rest, vᵢ = 0; for a body thrown upward, g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

rubric.why: The equations must be adapted to gravitational acceleration.
rubric.description: Explain how to adapt the equations of motion.
rubric.how: Say that a is replaced by g.

rubric.why: A clear downward-positive sign convention prevents sign errors.
rubric.description: State the sign convention for downward motion.
rubric.how: Take g positive downward and opposite-direction quantities as negative.

rubric.why: A released body starts from rest.
rubric.description: State the initial velocity for a body released from a height.
rubric.how: Write that vᵢ = 0 when it is released.

rubric.why: Upward motion requires the opposite sign for gravity and has zero velocity at its highest point.
rubric.description: State the conditions for a body thrown upward.
rubric.how: Say g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

modelAnswer: Since freely falling bodies move vertically downwards in a straight line with uniform acceleration g, the three equations of motion can be applied.
Replace acceleration a by gravitational acceleration g in the equations of motion:
v_f = v_i + gt
S = v_i t + ½gt²
2gS = v_f² − v_i²
Take g positive downward; quantities opposite to the acceleration are negative.
For a body released from a height, vᵢ = 0.
For a body thrown vertically upward, g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

written.text: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. How long will it take to reach the ground? What will be its velocity just before hitting the ground?

rubric.why: The known values and direction establish the correct free-fall setup.
rubric.description: State the initial conditions and known distance.
rubric.how: Write vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻² and S = 45 m.

rubric.why: The second equation of motion determines the fall time.
rubric.description: Find the time taken to reach the ground.
rubric.how: Use S = vᵢt + ½gt² and obtain 3 s.

rubric.why: The first equation of motion determines the velocity just before impact.
rubric.description: Find the velocity before hitting the ground.
rubric.how: Use v_f = vᵢ + gt and obtain 30 m s⁻¹ downward.

modelAnswer: For freely falling body: vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻², S = 45 m, t = ?, v_f = ?
According to second equation of motion, S = vᵢt + ½gt²
t² = 9, so t = 3 s
From the first equation of motion, v_f = vᵢ + gt
v_f = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m s⁻¹ downward
Answer: 3 s, 30 m s⁻¹

written.text: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 seconds. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.

rubric.why: The body is dropped, so it starts from rest, and the given time sets the calculation.
rubric.description: State the known values.
rubric.how: Write vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻² and t = 5 s.

rubric.why: The second equation gives the tower's height.
rubric.description: Calculate the height.
rubric.how: Use S = vᵢt + ½gt² to obtain 125 m.

rubric.why: The first equation gives the ball's velocity at impact.
rubric.description: Calculate the striking velocity.
rubric.how: Use v_f = vᵢ + gt to obtain 50 m s⁻¹ downward.

modelAnswer: For freely falling body: vᵢ = 0, g = 10 m s⁻², t = 5 s, S = h = ?, v_f = ?
According to second equation of motion, S = vᵢt + ½gt²
From the first equation of motion, v_f = vᵢ + gt
v_f = 0 + 10 × 5 = 50 m s⁻¹ downward
Answer: 125 m, 50 m s⁻¹

written.text: A cricket ball is hit so that it travels straight up in the air. An observer notes that it took 3 seconds to reach the highest point. What was the initial velocity of the ball? If the ball was hit 1 m above the ground, how high did it rise from the ground?

rubric.why: At the highest point velocity is zero and gravity is negative for upward motion.
rubric.description: Set the upward-motion values and signs.
rubric.how: Write v_f = 0, g = −10 m s⁻² and t = 3 s.

rubric.why: The first equation gives the initial velocity from the time to the highest point.
rubric.description: Find the initial velocity.
rubric.how: Use v_f = vᵢ + gt to obtain 30 m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: The third equation gives the ball's upward displacement from its launch point.
rubric.description: Find the rise above the point where it was hit.
rubric.how: Use 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ² to obtain 45 m.

rubric.why: The launch point is already 1 m above the ground, so it must be added to the upward displacement.
rubric.description: Find the maximum height above the ground.
rubric.how: Add 1 m to 45 m to obtain 46 m.

modelAnswer: For the ball moving vertically upward: v_f = 0, g = −10 m s⁻², t = 3 s, vᵢ = ?, S = ?
From first equation of motion, v_f = vᵢ + gt
Now from the third equation of motion, 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ²
Height above ground = 45 m + 1 m = 46 m
Answer: 30 m s⁻¹, 46 m

examTips: A numerical may describe an object dropped from a height and ask for its height, time, or impact velocity. Write the known values first, then show the equation and substitution.
For an object released from rest, state vᵢ = 0. Use g = 10 m s⁻² downward, as in your textbook.
For an object thrown upward, use g = −10 m s⁻² and v_f = 0 at the highest point.
Marks are commonly earned for the correct sign convention, choosing the suitable equation, substituting values, and giving a final answer with units.
Include the direction in a velocity answer when it is useful, such as downward or upward.

explain.title: Gravitational acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “When a body is falling freely under the action of gravity of the Earth, the acceleration acting on it is the gravitational acceleration and is denoted by g.” It also states: “The direction of gravitational acceleration is always downwards. Its value is 9.8 m s⁻², but for convenience we shall use the value of g as 10 m s⁻².”

explain.title: Equations for freely falling bodies
explain.body: The three equations of motion are used with a replaced by g: v_f = v_i + gt; S = v_i t + ½gt²; 2gS = v_f² − v_i². Choose the equation that includes the unknown you need.

explain.title: Choose signs carefully
explain.body: Use g as positive when downward is positive. Quantities in the opposite direction are negative. If a body is released from a height, vᵢ = 0. If it is thrown vertically upward, g is negative and the final velocity at the highest point is zero.

explain.title: Objects fall with the same acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Acceleration of free fall g is 10 m s⁻² for all objects.” The section also notes that light and heavier objects fall side by side through a vacuum.

mistakes: Using g = +10 m s⁻² for a body thrown upward; in that case use g = −10 m s⁻².
Forgetting that a body released from rest has vᵢ = 0.
Using a non-zero final velocity at the highest point; there v_f = 0.
Giving a velocity without a unit or using the wrong unit; velocity is measured in m s⁻¹ and acceleration in m s⁻².
Forgetting that the stated height for an upward-thrown object may be the rise above its starting point, not its height above the ground.
